slides.text: Seeing Gandhi going in the third class, the public got emotional after realising his simplicity and people became convinced that only Gandhi can lead the poor and downtrodden Indian people properly.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Raipur railway platform, December 20, 1920. Gandhi in dhoti and bandage kurta standing at the door of the third-class compartment, hands folded in namaste, the train still moving slowly. A sea of faces below. Ink-wash, sepia and gold.

slides.text: December 20, 1920. Raipur railway station. Every leader of the district is on the platform. Every volunteer has a position. Every garland is ready. The postal train from Calcutta is expected. The crowd has been here since before dawn.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station in the early morning of December 20, 1920. Platform packed. Volunteers in position. Garlands of marigold waiting. Leaders at the front — Shukla, Pyarelal Singh, Sakharam Dubey. The crowd pressing forward. A city holding its breath.

slides.text: The train arrives. First class doors open: Dadasaheb Khaparde, Dr. Munje, and other prominent leaders descend. The crowd scans their faces. Gandhi is not among them. Second class — no Gandhi. A wave of confusion passes through the platform.
slides.visualDescription: The train pulling in. First-class doors opening — Khaparde, Munje descending. The crowd searching. No Gandhi. Second class — same. The confusion of a crowd that prepared for one moment and is suddenly unsure. Where is he? Where is Gandhi?

slides.text: Then: someone says it — he is in the third-class compartment. The crowd turns and surges toward the far end of the train. What they see stops them. Gandhi in a Lungi and Bandage Kurta, standing at the door with folded hands. The train still moving.
slides.visualDescription: The moment of recognition — the crowd turning, surging to the third-class end of the train. Then stopping. Gandhi at the door: simple cloth, folded hands, gentle eyes. The train still rolling. The crowd stilled by what it sees. Simplicity as revelation.

slides.text: As eyewitness Prabhu Lal Kabra recorded: 'Gandhi, wearing a Lungi and Bandage Kurta, was standing at the door of the third-class compartment with folded hands, till then the train started moving.' The train was in motion as Gandhi greeted Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: Prabhu Lal Kabra as a young man in the crowd — witnessing, recording in his memory what he will write about for the rest of his life. His eyewitness account as text beside the scene. The historian in the crowd. The moment preserved through one man's memory.

slides.text: Seeing Gandhi going in third class, the public got emotional. This man — this leader of the nation — chose to sit where the poorest sat. Not as a gesture, but as a way of life. In that choice, Chhattisgarh understood everything about him.
slides.visualDescription: The third-class compartment interior — wooden benches, crowded, no cushions. Then Gandhi visible within it as if he belongs. The contrast: first-class compartment in the same frame, plush and empty. Gandhi's choice as a statement louder than any speech.

slides.text: Gandhi was lodged at Barrister Thakkar's bungalow in Raipur. The Ali brothers — Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali — stayed with him. The leaders of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement gathered in the bungalow courtyard. The first day had begun.
slides.visualDescription: Barrister Thakkar's bungalow — a fine colonial structure. Gandhi welcomed at the entrance. The Ali brothers arriving. Ravi Shankar Shukla, Pt. Sharma, Srivastava, Pyarelal Singh gathered in the courtyard. A room full of history, waiting for the moment.

slides.text: That evening: the massive public meeting at the ground near Kankalipara — what would become Gandhi Chowk. About fifteen thousand people gathered. The whole district had come to one place, to hear one man speak for the first time.
slides.visualDescription: Kankalipara ground filling with people as evening comes. Fifteen thousand faces lit by torches and lamps. The stage prepared. The Ali brothers taking their places. Gandhi approaching the podium. The ground shaking slightly with the weight of the gathering.

slides.text: Shaukat Ali spoke first, introducing himself with humour: 'I am like an elephant and Gandhi is like a goat.' The crowd laughed. Then his deeper point: 'Even if I die, it will not be of any use, but Gandhi is still useful for everyone.'
slides.visualDescription: Shaukat Ali towering at the podium — his size and presence filling the stage. Gandhi seated beside him, small and still. The crowd laughing at the elephant-goat comparison, then growing thoughtful as the deeper meaning arrives. Wit becoming wisdom.

slides.text: Then Gandhi stood and spoke. He outlined the Non-Cooperation Movement. He spoke of Swaraj — self-rule — not as a distant dream but as an immediate practical commitment. He spread his bag for the Tilak Swaraj Fund.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Kankalipara podium — his voice measured, his presence immense despite his small frame. The Tilak Fund bag spread open before him. The crowd pressing forward with money, jewelry, silver. A practical collection in service of an immense idea.

slides.text: At the women's gathering in Machilabad, Tatyapara — a large number of Muslim women attended openly. They donated to the Tilak Fund publicly. Hindu and Muslim women, standing on the same ground, giving from the same impulse. Unity made material.
slides.visualDescription: The women's gathering in Machilabad — Muslim women in purdah and Hindu women in saris standing together. Gold bangles and silver rings being placed in the Tilak Fund bag. Hands of different communities reaching toward the same purpose. Unity visible.

slides.text: Gandhi visited the Jaitasava monastery that evening. The meeting of activist and monastery — the political and the spiritual sharing the same December night in Raipur. Gandhi moved through both worlds with equal ease and equal reverence.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Jaitasava monastery — an ancient, lamp-lit space. He removes his sandals at the entrance. The monks receiving him with folded hands. The meeting of two kinds of dedication: political and spiritual, both in service of the same truth.

slides.text: The Raipur District Congress Committee was formed that same evening. Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla was made its first secretary. A permanent structure of resistance — not dependent on any one person's visit, but capable of sustaining the movement long after Gandhi leaves.
slides.visualDescription: The founding of the Raipur DCC — Shukla signing by lamplight, Gandhi's hand on his shoulder. The document: the founding charter. An institution born from a single night's meeting. Chhattisgarh organising itself permanently. History being made quietly.

slides.text: The next morning — December 21 — Abbas Bhai's motor waited at Azad Chowk. Destination: Dhamtari. On receiving information about Gandhi's arrival, irrigation officials had already withdrawn the anti-farmer order. The Satyagraha had won. Gandhi was still going.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai's motor at Azad Chowk at dawn, December 21. Gandhi and the Ali brothers boarding. The news of the canal order's withdrawal already spreading among the crowd. The Satyagraha won — but the visit continues. Going to honour what was earned.

slides.text: The road to Dhamtari: people lining both sides from Raipur all the way to the destination. Villages emptied as people came to the road. Children in trees. Women on rooftops. Farmers leaving their fields. A nation refusing to miss this moment.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur-Dhamtari road as a human corridor — people ten deep on both sides. The motor moving through them slowly. Flowers thrown. Abbas Bhai navigating carefully. Gandhi's hand raised continuously. Every person trying to catch Gandhi's eye for a single moment.

slides.text: Makai Chowk, Dhamtari. Within Seth Hussain's enclosure — a crowd beyond count. The motor cannot approach the stage. At that moment, Omar Seth — a businessman from Gurur — stepped forward and lifted Gandhi onto his shoulders.
slides.visualDescription: Makai Chowk — packed wall to wall. Omar Seth of Gurur — powerful, decisive — lifting Gandhi onto his shoulders and carrying him through the crowd to the stage. Gandhi above the sea of heads, hand raised. The crowd parting slightly, then closing again behind them.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke for an hour at Dhamtari. He praised Chhotelal Babu, Narayan Rao Meghawale, and Pt. Sundarlal Sharma by name. He made the heroes of the Kandel Satyagraha known to 15,000 people who had gathered to see him.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi speaking at the Dhamtari podium. His voice carrying across the enormous crowd. He points to Chhotelal Srivastava in the crowd — naming him. Naming Meghawale. Naming Sharma. The act of naming as the highest honour. Heroes made visible.

slides.text: Bajirao Kridatta presented Rs 501 to Gandhi. More than 500 activists committed to attend the Nagpur session. The movement was not just heard — it was joined. Dhamtari chose, publicly and formally, to be part of what India was becoming.
slides.visualDescription: Kridatta presenting the bag of Rs 501. Gandhi accepting with both hands. Five hundred raised hands for Nagpur. The joining formal and public. Dhamtari — the city of the Kandel Satyagraha — now formally in the national movement. Commitment visible.

slides.text: The return journey from Dhamtari to Raipur. The same roads, the same crowds. Abbas Bhai at the wheel. Gandhi quiet in the back seat, perhaps aware that he has been present at the birth of something he cannot fully measure yet.
slides.visualDescription: The return journey in the evening light. Abbas Bhai driving. Gandhi in the back seat looking out at the passing landscape — the fields, the villages, the people still lining the road to see him pass. Quiet. Contemplative. The land receiving him.

slides.text: Evening in Raipur. The massive Kankalipara meeting. A drama had played on this stage the night before — Bhishma Pitamah. Now it holds Gandhi. After the meeting, people took bricks from the stage as mementos until the stage itself was gone.
slides.visualDescription: The Kankalipara stage being dismantled by devotion — brick by brick, people taking pieces of the wood and earth that Gandhi stood on. The stage disappearing into a thousand hands. Sacred objects made from ordinary materials by the touch of one man.

slides.text: That night, the Raipur District Congress Committee founding was formally completed. Ravi Shankar Shukla signed as first secretary. What had been informal resistance was now a formal organisation — accountable, structured, permanent.
slides.visualDescription: Late night in Raipur — the DCC founding documents signed. Shukla, Sharma, Pyarelal Singh, Srivastava around a table by lamplight. Gandhi present but not presiding — this is theirs, not his. The organisation that will carry his work when he is gone.

slides.text: December 22, 1920. The third and final day of Gandhi's first visit to Chhattisgarh. The morning of departure. Gandhi at Raipur station, bag in hand, the familiar simplicity of the man who arrived in third class preparing to leave the same way.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station, morning of December 22. Gandhi at the platform with his small bag. No ceremony beyond what the crowd provides. The leaders seeing him off. Some faces showing what they cannot say: will he come back? When will we see him again?

slides.text: Gandhi boards the Nagpur-bound train. He boards third class. The crowd watches until the train is out of sight. Three days — a Satyagraha honoured, a committee founded, 15,000 mobilised twice, the Tilak Fund enriched, and a province changed.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi boarding the third-class compartment for Nagpur — the same simplicity as his arrival. The crowd on the platform. The train pulling away. The crowd watching until nothing is visible. The departure that will echo for thirty more years.

slides.text: What remained? The Raipur DCC. The 500 committed to Nagpur. The bricks from the Kankalipara stage in people's homes. The names of Srivastava, Meghawale, Sharma now known beyond their villages. The memory of a man in a third-class compartment.
slides.visualDescription: The aftermath of Gandhi's first visit: a brick from the Kankalipara stage on a family's altar, the DCC headquarters sign being put up, Srivastava being greeted differently in his village now. The residue of greatness distributed across many lives.

slides.text: Lawyers who had attended the meetings began discussions about leaving their practices. Titleholders began reconsidering their British honours. Teachers began organising national schools. The Non-Cooperation Movement was no longer a resolution — it was a way of life beginning.
slides.visualDescription: The movement spreading after Gandhi's departure — lawyers discussing in their offices, a titleholder removing his colonial medal, teachers organising. The ripple effect of three days spreading outward through weeks and months. Action following inspiration.

slides.text: The Nagpur Congress session of December 26, 1920. The Non-Cooperation resolution passed. Five hundred from Dhamtari voted for it. Chhattisgarh was not a province receiving the national movement — it was a province shaping it with its own votes and voices.
slides.visualDescription: The Nagpur Congress session — a massive gathering. 500 delegates from Dhamtari visible among thousands. The Non-Cooperation resolution being read and voted on. Chhattisgarh's hands among the thousands raised in assent. The province choosing its destiny.

slides.text: Vamanrao Lakhe surrendered his Rai Sahab title on the very day it was announced at the Nagpur Congress. The people of Raipur immediately gave him the title of Popular. What the British had given in honor was surrendered; what the people gave was kept.
slides.visualDescription: Vamanrao Lakhe surrendering his Rai Sahab medal — placing it on a table before a British officer. Walking out. Then: the people of Raipur garlanding him with the title Popular. Two titles: one from empire, surrendered; one from the people, accepted.

slides.text: Thakur Pyarelal Singh and Ramdayal Tiwari left the practice of law. Barrister Thakkar — in whose bungalow Gandhi had stayed — boycotted the assembly elections he was standing for. The men closest to Gandhi's visit paid the highest personal prices.
slides.visualDescription: Pyarelal Singh and Tiwari closing their law offices — hanging up their barrister's robes. Barrister Thakkar withdrawing his election papers. The cost of proximity to Gandhi's ideas made concrete in three men's professional lives. Sacrifice as commitment.

slides.text: National schools were established. Madhav Rao Sapre in Raipur, Chhotelal Srivastava in Dhamtari, Badrinath Saw in Bilaspur. Education as a weapon of the Non-Cooperation Movement — refusing British schools, building Indian ones.
slides.visualDescription: Three national schools opening simultaneously — Sapre's in Raipur, Srivastava's in Dhamtari, Saw's in Bilaspur. Children pouring in through new gates. Teachers unafraid of British disapproval. Education as an act of non-cooperation. Learning as resistance.

slides.text: Mohammad Yunus, told to pay tax or go to jail, said to the judge: 'I am involved in Mahatma Gandhi's non-cooperation movement from now on.' He went directly from court to jail. His seventeen-village zamindari, hundreds of acres, cattle, and gold were all confiscated.
slides.visualDescription: Mohammad Yunus before the British judge — calm, dignified, making his declaration. The judge's pen poised. Yunus turning from court to jail without hesitation. His zamindari — seventeen villages, hundreds of acres — disappearing into British confiscation behind him.

slides.text: Abbas Bhai received the notice of his transport license cancellation. His Raipur Bus Service was shut down. He had driven Gandhi to Dhamtari. For this, he paid with his livelihood. He is among the most ordinary and most complete of all the heroes in this story.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai reading the license cancellation notice outside his shuttered Raipur Bus Service office. His motor parked behind him, unable to operate. The quiet tragedy of the ordinary man who paid for a single act of solidarity with everything he had built.

slides.text: Prabhu Lal Kabra and Ratnakar Jha took out a huge procession to boycott foreign goods on August 1, 1921. The movement had moved from platform and podium to the streets. Gandhi's three days had become Chhattisgarh's permanent commitment.
slides.visualDescription: August 1, 1921. Kabra and Jha leading a procession through Raipur — a long line of people carrying khadi, burning foreign cloth, marching in discipline. The movement in the streets. Gandhi's platform moment become a daily practice across the province.

slides.text: Three days. That is all Gandhi spent in Chhattisgarh on his first visit. Three days in December 1920. And from those three days: a DCC, a Satyagraha honoured, 500 delegates committed, schools founded, lawyers resigned, titles surrendered.
slides.visualDescription: A visual inventory of everything Gandhi's three days produced: the DCC banner, the Kandel canal flowing free, the Nagpur delegates, the national schools, the surrendered titles, the burned foreign cloth. Three days made into years of consequence.

slides.text: He came as Mohandas. He left as something more in the hearts of Chhattisgarh. Not yet The Mahatma — that would come later — but already the proof that a man who travels third class, who listens before he speaks, can move a province.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's departing train against the Chhattisgarh landscape — small on the horizon, growing smaller. But in the people left behind: something lit. The man diminishing in physical distance, growing in importance in every heart that watched him go.

slides.text: The women of Chhattisgarh were part of this from the beginning — the gathering at Machilabad, the Muslim women donating openly, the bricks of the Kankalipara stage carried home by their hands. The movement was never just male. It was never just one community.
slides.visualDescription: The women of the first visit: at Machilabad donating gold, at Kankalipara carrying bricks, at Dhamtari listening to Gandhi praise Srivastava. Women present at every moment of Gandhi's Chhattisgarh visit — seen, active, essential. Not peripheral. Central.

slides.text: Gandhi would not return to Chhattisgarh for thirteen years. But the movement he touched would not pause. The decade between 1920 and 1933 — filled with Jungle Satyagrahas, civil disobedience, Salt March echoes — would build Chhattisgarh into something stronger.
slides.visualDescription: The calendar advancing from December 1920 — each year marked with an event in Chhattisgarh: 1922 Jungle Satyagraha, 1923 Jhanda Satyagraha, 1930 Salt March, 1932 Civil Disobedience. Thirteen years of movement building toward the Mahatma's return.

slides.text: The day in Dhamtari cannot end without one more telling. Omar Seth carried Gandhi on his shoulders. A businessman from Gurur, a crowd of thousands, one man strong enough to lift what the crowd could not move. Next: Episode 9 — The Day in Dhamtari.
slides.visualDescription: Omar Seth's shoulders — Gandhi above the crowd at Makai Chowk. The image held. The visual that Dhamtari will carry forever. Title card fading in: Episode 9 — The Day in Dhamtari.
